questions.q: A collision between two isolated objects occurs, but some kinetic energy becomes heat. Which statement can still remain true?
options: Total momentum is conserved even though kinetic energy is not.
Both momentum and kinetic energy must decrease.
Kinetic energy conservation requires momentum to change.
Heat production prevents conservation of momentum.
questions.why: Momentum is conserved in an isolated system; kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

questions.q: A planet's orbit becomes more elliptical after an interaction. At which part of the orbit is its speed greatest?
options: At its closest approach to the Sun
At its greatest distance from the Sun
At every point equally
Only when it crosses Earth's orbital plane
questions.why: An orbiting object moves faster when nearer the Sun, consistent with conservation of orbital energy and angular momentum.

questions.q: A spectrum from a star has absorption lines at the same pattern of wavelengths as a laboratory element but shifted together. What does the shared pattern indicate?
options: The element can be present in the star, while the shift can reveal relative motion.
The star must be made only of that element.
The element's lines are caused by the telescope's mirror shape.
The shift directly gives the star's distance without other information.
questions.why: Line patterns identify atoms or molecules, and a common shift can indicate Doppler motion.

questions.q: Two thermal sources have peaks at different wavelengths. Which source has the higher surface temperature?
options: The source whose spectrum peaks at the shorter wavelength
The source whose spectrum peaks at the longer wavelength
The source with the smaller apparent size, regardless of spectrum
Neither; peak wavelength contains no temperature information
questions.why: A hotter thermal source has its peak emission at a shorter wavelength.

questions.q: An atom emits a photon as an electron moves from a higher energy level to a lower one. Which statement must be true?
options: The photon carries energy equal to the difference between the levels.
The electron gains energy from the photon while moving downward.
The photon must be a radio wave regardless of the level spacing.
The atom's number of protons changes.
questions.why: The emitted photon carries the energy lost as the electron transitions between levels.

questions.q: A galaxy's spectral lines are shifted toward longer wavelengths. Which conclusion is best supported before other effects are considered?
options: The galaxy is receding along our line of sight.
The galaxy must be rotating so rapidly that it is breaking apart.
The galaxy is moving only across the sky with no radial motion.
The shift proves that its temperature is increasing.
questions.why: A redshift indicates motion away along the line of sight, though cosmological expansion can also contribute.

questions.q: A star's spectrum contains broad absorption features from both the star and Earth's atmosphere. What should an astronomer do to separate the sources?
options: Compare with reference or calibration observations of the atmosphere.
Assume every absorption feature came from the star.
Replace spectroscopy with a single colour image.
Use only the star's apparent position.
questions.why: The atmosphere can imprint absorption features, so calibration helps distinguish terrestrial from astronomical signals.

questions.q: A larger telescope produces a brighter image of a dim galaxy, but the galaxy's apparent size is unchanged. Which statement best explains this?
options: Aperture improves light collection; image scale and magnification are separate properties.
The aperture cannot affect recorded brightness.
The detector has become a gravitational-wave instrument.
The galaxy's physical size has changed.
questions.why: Aperture collects more light, while magnification and image scale address apparent size.

questions.q: An observatory combines two separated radio dishes and can distinguish a close pair of sources better than either dish alone. What has primarily improved?
options: Angular resolution from the longer effective baseline
The sum of the dish areas beyond their physical sizes
The atmosphere's transmission of X-rays
The intrinsic brightness of both sources
questions.why: Interferometry uses separation between telescopes to improve resolving power without enlarging each dish.

questions.q: A telescope's detector records a sharp image only when placed at one precise location behind the optics. What is that location?
options: The focal plane
The celestial equator
The horizon
The transmission window
questions.why: The focal plane is where incoming rays from a source are brought into focus.

questions.q: An orbit diagram shows Mercury, the asteroid belt, Jupiter, and a distant icy population in that order. Which interpretation best matches the solar-system structure?
options: Rocky inner planets precede the asteroid belt and outer giant planets, with icy bodies beyond.
The asteroid belt lies beyond the Oort cloud.
All icy bodies orbit inside Mercury's path.
The diagram proves the planets' sizes are drawn to scale.
questions.why: The broad order of the regions is inner rocky planets, asteroid belt, outer planets, and distant small-body populations.

questions.q: A world is similar to Earth in size but has a dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere and extreme surface heating. Which comparison is most useful?
options: Venus shows that similar size does not guarantee similar surface conditions.
Jupiter shows that rocky planets cannot retain atmospheres.
Mercury shows that every dense atmosphere causes extreme heating.
Neptune shows that all inner planets are ice giants.
questions.why: Venus and Earth are similar in size but have very different atmospheres and surface environments.

questions.q: A comet becomes active near the Sun and its tail points away from the Sun while the nucleus moves in another direction. Which process best accounts for this geometry?
options: Solar heating releases gas and dust that radiation and solar wind push outward.
The tail is a solid extension trailing the comet's velocity.
The comet's gravity bends its own tail toward the Sun.
The nucleus is pushed backward by Earth's atmosphere.
questions.why: Released gas and dust are pushed away from the Sun, so the tail direction is not simply behind the comet's motion.

questions.q: Which observation is the strongest evidence for a rotating disk during solar-system formation?
options: Most planets orbit in nearly the same plane and direction.
Every planet has the same number of moons.
All planets have exactly equal densities.
Every comet has a visible tail throughout its orbit.
questions.why: A flattened rotating disk naturally explains the coordinated orbital directions and planes.

questions.q: A small rocky body is round and orbits the Sun, but it shares its orbital neighborhood with many other sizable objects. Which classification is most appropriate?
options: Dwarf planet
Major planet
Natural satellite
Cometary coma
questions.why: A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is nearly round but has not cleared its orbital neighborhood.

questions.q: A spacecraft must compare a surface mineral at one location with the composition of the planet as a whole. Which pairing provides the most complementary evidence?
options: A lander or rover for local analysis and an orbiter for broad mapping
Two flybys with no instruments
A light curve alone and a larger display screen
A terrestrial telescope and a clock
questions.why: Surface missions provide local measurements, while orbiters give repeated broad coverage.

questions.q: A space observatory detects radiation absorbed by Earth's atmosphere, while a ground telescope continues visible-light observations. Which conclusion follows?
options: Space and ground observatories provide complementary wavelength access.
Ground telescopes cannot collect any electromagnetic radiation.
The atmosphere blocks every wavelength equally.
The space observatory changes the source's emission.
questions.why: Ground instruments remain valuable in atmospheric windows, while space telescopes can access blocked wavelengths.

tests.title: ASTR 207 Challenge Practice
tests.blurb: 12 multi-step questions on sky motions, Newton's laws, orbits, light, spectra, and telescopes.

tests.title: Practice Exam 5: Telescopes and Our Planetary System
tests.blurb: 48 questions on lenses, mirrors and telescopes, light across the spectrum, then the Sun, planets, moons and small bodies.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the lens in an eye?
options: to prevent dust and irritants from entering the eye
to bend light entering the eye so that it is focused onto the retina
to adjust the amount of light entering the eye
to send optical signals to the brain to be interpreted
to separate the light collected by the eye into colours
questions.why: The lens of the eye bends (refracts) incoming light so that it comes to a focus on the retina, where the image is detected. Adjusting how much light enters is the job of the iris and pupil, not the lens. Eyelids, lashes and tears keep out dust, and the retina and optic nerve (not the lens) send the signals to the brain. The eye does not split light into colours.
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q1; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48)

questions.q: Which of the following is used in a lens to focus light into an image?
options: Refraction
Transmission
Absorption
Diffraction
Reflection
questions.why: A lens focuses light by refraction: light changes direction as it passes from air into curved glass, so parallel rays are bent to meet at a focus. Transmission only means light passes through, and absorption removes light instead of focusing it. Reflection is what a mirror uses, not a lens. Diffraction is the spreading of waves at edges, which limits how sharp an image can be but does not form it.
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q2; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48)

questions.q: What is the benefit of a longer exposure time when making an image?
options: It allows the detector to collect more total light.
It allows the detector to achieve higher angular resolution.
It allows the detector to measure rapid variations in light intensity.
It allows the detector to record light at very short wavelengths.
questions.why: A longer exposure lets the detector keep adding up light from a faint source, so it records more total light and can reveal dimmer objects. Angular resolution depends on the telescope's diameter and the wavelength, not on how long you expose. Following rapid changes in brightness needs short exposures, not long ones, and which wavelengths can be recorded depends on the detector itself.
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q3; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48)

questions.q: How does the light-collecting area of a telescope with a 10-meter diameter mirror compare to that of a telescope with a 5-meter diameter mirror?
options: The 10-meter telescope has 4 times the light collecting area.
The 10-meter telescope has 2 times the light collecting area.
The 10-meter telescope has 10 times the light collecting area.
questions.why: Light-collecting area depends on the square of the diameter, because area = π(D/2)². Going from 5 m to 10 m doubles the diameter, so the area is 2² = 4 times larger. A factor of 2 is just the ratio of the diameters, which is the usual slip, and a factor of 10 would need a mirror 10 times wider than the small one.
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q4; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48)

questions.q: How does the best possible angular resolution of a telescope with a 10-meter diameter mirror compare to that of a telescope with a 5-meter diameter mirror?
options: The 10-meter telescope's angular resolution is better by a factor of 2.
The 10-meter telescope's angular resolution is better by a factor of 4.
The 10-meter telescope's angular resolution is better by a factor of 10.
questions.why: The best angular resolution (the diffraction limit) is proportional to the wavelength divided by the diameter. Doubling the diameter from 5 m to 10 m therefore halves the smallest angle the telescope can separate, so its resolution is better by a factor of 2. The factor of 4 belongs to light-collecting area, not to resolution, and nothing makes the improvement tenfold.
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q5; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48)

questions.q: Suppose two stars are separated in the sky by 0.1 arcseconds. If you take a picture of them with the SOAR telescope, which has an angular resolution of 0.6 arcsecond, what will you see?
options: nothing at all
two separate points of light
one point of light that is the blurred image of both stars
questions.why: SOAR can only separate objects that are more than about 0.6 arcsecond apart. These two stars are just 0.1 arcsecond apart, six times closer than that limit, so their images overlap and merge into one blurred spot of light. Blurring does not make the light disappear, so you would still see something. Two separate points would require a resolution of 0.1 arcsecond or better.
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q6; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48)

questions.q: If you want to see the image formed by a telescope, you should place your eye at the location of the telescope's
options: Cassegrain.
focus.
secondary mirror.
primary mirror.
central hole in the primary mirror.
questions.why: A telescope brings light to a focus, and the image exists at that point, so that is where an eyepiece (or your eye) must be placed to see it. The primary and secondary mirrors only collect and redirect the light. A Cassegrain is a type of telescope design, and the hole in the primary mirror is just a passage the light travels through on its way to the focus.
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q7; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48)

questions.q: Which of the following is one important reason why most large astronomical telescopes are reflecting telescopes rather than refracting telescopes?
options: Reflecting telescopes have their heaviest component (the mirror) at the bottom rather than the top of the telescope's tube.
Reflecting telescopes take up less space than refracting telescopes.
Reflecting telescopes are taller than refracting telescopes.
For a mirror and lens of the same diameter, a mirror will collect more light.
questions.why: A big mirror sits at the bottom of the tube and can be supported across its whole back, while a big lens sits at the top and can be held only around its edge, so it sags under its own weight. That support problem is a major reason why giant telescopes are reflectors. A mirror and a lens of the same diameter collect the same amount of light, so that option is wrong. Reflectors are not taller, and being more compact is a side benefit, not what makes very large telescopes possible.
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q8; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48); key 0 matches the reason given in the book (mirror mounted at the bottom, large lens held only at its edge, p. 170, PDF p. 192; Ch6.2_pt1 slides 8-9)

questions.q: Which of the following measurements can be made only by recording and comparing the amount of light received from an astronomical source at many different times?
options: the rate at which a variable star brightens and dims
the color of a planet
the general shape of an interstellar cloud of gas
the number of bright stars in a nearby star cluster
questions.why: To find how fast a variable star brightens and dims you have to measure its brightness again and again and compare the measurements over time. The colour of a planet, the shape of a gas cloud and the number of bright stars in a cluster can all be found from a single image taken at one moment.
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q9; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48)

questions.q: Which of the following could not be determined by an observation that only uses spectroscopy?
options: the chemical composition of a distant star
the speed at which a distant galaxy is moving away from us
the surface temperature of a distant star
the rotation rate of a distant star
the angular size of a distant galaxy
questions.why: A spectrum spreads light out by wavelength, but it is not an image, so it cannot tell you how large an object appears on the sky. Spectral lines still reveal composition (which lines appear), temperature (the shape of the spectrum and which lines are strong), the Doppler shift that gives how fast a galaxy recedes, and rotation (spinning broadens the lines).
questions.source: admin-only: student's Assignment 5 (optics, telescopes and our planetary system) Q10; key = the option the student selected and scored correct (48/48)

questions.q: What is meant by spectral resolution?
options: It is a measure of how close two stars can be in the sky and still be distinguishable.
It is a measure of how close two spectral lines can be and still be distinguishable.
It is a measure of how much energy an object emits in different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
It is the same as angular resolution but applied to telescopes operating at different wavelengths.
questions.why: Spectral resolution describes how well a spectrograph can tell two nearby wavelengths apart, meaning how close two spectral lines can be and still be seen as separate lines. How close two stars can be in the sky is angular resolution. Energy emitted at different wavelengths is the spectrum itself, not its resolution, and spectral resolution is not just angular resolution at other wavelengths.

questions.q: What do astronomers mean by light pollution?
options: Light pollution refers to pollution caused by light industry as opposed to heavy industry.
Light pollution refers to harmful gases emitted by common street lights.
Light pollution refers to light used for human activities that brightens the sky and hinders astronomical observations.
Light pollution refers to the lights that must be used inside major observatories and that make it difficult for astronomers' eyes to adapt to darkness.
Light pollution is another name for sunlight, which makes it impossible to see stars in the daytime.
questions.why: Light pollution is stray artificial light from cities, streets and buildings that brightens the night sky and washes out faint astronomical objects. It has nothing to do with light industry, harmful gases from lamps or the lights inside an observatory, and sunlight in the daytime is a natural effect, not pollution.

questions.q: What causes stars to twinkle?
options: The human eye has difficulty seeing faint objects.
Interstellar gas along the line of sight to the star absorbs different amounts of radiation.
Moving gases in Earth's atmosphere randomly bend light rays from stars.
Stars constantly vary in brightness as they expand and contract.
questions.why: Twinkling happens because pockets of air in Earth's atmosphere are constantly moving, and they randomly bend the starlight in slightly different directions from moment to moment. That makes the star's brightness and position flicker. It is not a weakness of the eye, and stars that are pulsing change over days or longer, not many times a second. Gas between the stars does not flicker on this time scale.

questions.q: What is the purpose of adaptive optics?
options: to increase the collecting area of telescopes on the ground
to reduce the distorting effects of atmospheric turbulence for telescopes on the ground
to allow several small telescopes to work together like a single larger telescope
to increase the magnification of telescopes on the ground
to improve the angular resolution of telescopes in space
questions.why: Adaptive optics uses a flexible mirror, adjusted many times each second, to cancel the blurring that turbulent air causes, so a ground telescope gets much sharper images. It does not enlarge the collecting area, combine separate telescopes (that is interferometry), or add magnification. Space telescopes are above the air and do not need it.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a good reason to place an observatory on a remote mountain?

reduce the twinkling caused by Earth's atmosphere
reduce the impact of light pollution
allow observations at ultraviolet and x-ray wavelengths
questions.why: A remote mountaintop helps with infrared light (it is above most of the water vapour that absorbs it), with steadier images (less air above) and with darker skies away from city lights. It does not help with ultraviolet or x-rays, because the atmosphere blocks those wavelengths even at the summit, so they can only be observed from space.

questions.q: What is the best reason to put a visible-light telescope in space instead of on the ground?
options: Space telescopes are not affected by earthquakes.
A space telescope is closer to the source of the light, so it can make a clearer image.
The telescope is above the atmosphere so the light does not get distorted by turbulent air.
It is easier to launch very large space telescopes into space than to find places for them on the ground.
questions.why: Above the atmosphere there is no turbulent air to blur the light, so a space telescope can reach the sharpness its mirror allows. Being slightly closer to a star changes nothing, since the stars are trillions of kilometres away. Earthquakes are rarely the main problem on the ground, and launching a huge telescope is actually harder than building it on the ground.

x-rays.
ultraviolet light.
visible light.
radio waves.

Mirrors for shorter wavelengths have to be polished far more precisely, which limits their size.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes how and why x-ray telescopes differ from visible light telescopes?
options: X-ray telescopes use grazing incidence mirrors because x-ray photons will penetrate a normal mirror.
X-ray telescopes have to be built with very thick mirrors because x-ray photons will penetrate a thin mirror.
X-ray telescopes do not use mirrors because x-ray photons cannot be focused.
X-ray telescopes must be much larger because of the small number of x-ray photons.
X-ray telescopes cannot do spectroscopy because all x-ray photons have the same wavelength.
questions.why: X-ray photons carry so much energy that they would pass into an ordinary mirror instead of bouncing off. They can only be reflected if they skim the surface at a very shallow angle, so x-ray telescopes use nested grazing-incidence mirrors. They can be focused, they do not need thick mirrors, and x-ray photons come in many wavelengths, so spectroscopy is possible.

questions.q: What does the technique of interferometry allow?
options: It allows two or more telescopes to obtain a total light-collecting area much larger than the total light-collecting area of the individual telescopes.
It allows us to determine the chemical composition of stars.
It allows astronomers to make astronomical observations without interference from light pollution.
It allows the same telescope to make images with both radio waves and visible light.
It allows two or more telescopes to obtain the angular resolution of a single telescope much larger than any of the individual telescopes.
questions.why: Interferometry combines the signals from several telescopes so that together they achieve the angular resolution of one telescope as wide as the distance between them. It does not create extra light-collecting area (the total light collected is still the sum of the separate telescopes), and it has nothing to do with composition, light pollution or imaging in two kinds of waves.

questions.q: Astronomers sometimes make use of "neutrino telescopes," which are typically located deep underground. What are neutrinos?

a type of light-weight subatomic particle
a very low-energy form of light
a type of wave predicted to exist by Einstein's general theory of relativity
questions.why: Neutrinos are extremely light subatomic particles that hardly ever interact with matter, made in nuclear reactions in the Sun and in exploding stars. They are particles, not forms of light of any energy, and they are not the gravitational waves of general relativity. The detectors sit deep underground so that other particles are blocked and only the neutrinos get through.

questions.q: Are cosmic rays a form of light?
options: No, they consist of high-energy subatomic particles, not of electromagnetic waves.
Yes, they are the name we give to all rays of light that come from the cosmos.
Yes, they are light waves with higher energy than gamma rays.
Yes, they are light waves with lower energy than radio waves.
questions.why: Cosmic rays are fast-moving subatomic particles, mostly protons and atomic nuclei, not electromagnetic waves, so they are not light. Light of higher energy than gamma rays or lower energy than radio waves does not exist as a separate class, and the name does not mean all light from the cosmos.

questions.q: What are gravitational waves?
options: the name we give to electromagnetic waves that come from astronomical objects that have gravity
a type of energy that is different from light and that has been detected from sources such as merging neutron stars and black holes
a form of light with higher energy than gamma rays
a form of light with lower energy than radio waves
questions.why: Gravitational waves are ripples in space and time predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity. They are a different kind of signal from light, and they have been detected from merging black holes and merging neutron stars. They are not electromagnetic waves, so they cannot be light with more energy than gamma rays or less than radio waves.

questions.q: Which of the following indicates that past conditions on Mars may have been suitable for life?

Mars has polar caps.

questions.q: Which of the following observations of an extrasolar planet system would be inconsistent with what we expect from the nebular theory of solar system formation?
options: a system in which some planets have small moons orbiting in a direction opposite to the planet's rotation
a system which has two terrestrial planets close in and two jovian planets farther out
a system in which all the planets orbit in completely different planes
a system in which some planets rotate in a direction opposite to their orbits
questions.why: The nebular theory says planets form in a flat disk made when the collapsing cloud flattened, so planets should orbit in nearly the same plane. A system where every planet orbits in a completely different plane would contradict that. The other systems fit the theory: some small moons can be captured planetesimals orbiting the wrong way, rocky planets inside and gas giants outside is the pattern the frost line predicts, and a planet spinning against its orbit can come from a giant impact.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT evidence against the close encounter hypothesis of star system formation?
options: We observe the planets all orbiting in the same direction around the Sun.
The vast majority of stars have orbiting planets.
The composition of the Sun is very different from that of the planets.
We observe stars forming from protoplanetary disks in nebulae.
questions.why: Three of the statements are things the close encounter idea cannot explain. It could not account for the orderly motions of the planets, such as all orbiting the same way, or for planets that differ so much from the Sun (the Sun is nearly all hydrogen and helium, while the terrestrial planets are rock and metal). It also required a very rare near-collision between stars, which cannot explain the many planetary systems we see around most stars. Watching young stars form with disks in nebulae is different: it is direct support for the nebular theory rather than a failure of the close encounter idea itself.
