questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a step in the stellar recycling process?
options: Stars release their chemical contents at the end of their lives, either gradually in the form of a planetary nebula, or more violently in a supernova explosion.
Radioactivity breaks down the large nuclei of heavy elements, ensuring there is sufficient hydrogen and helium for future generations of stars.
Nuclear fusion within stars produces elements with higher atomic numbers, up to iron in some stars.
Nebulae collapse under gravity, forming new stars.
questions.why: Stellar recycling is: stars form in gas clouds, fusion builds heavier elements, dying stars return that material to space as a planetary nebula or supernova, and the enriched gas forms new stars. Radioactivity breaking down heavy nuclei is not a step, and hydrogen and helium were made in the Big Bang, not by decay. Fusion in stars building elements up to iron is a correct step.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q3 (no printed key); key checked: galactic recycling: Ch8.1 slide 5; p. 219 (PDF p. 241); key 1 confirmed

questions.q: Which of the following is most important in causing a cloud of gas to collapse to form a star and planets?
options: Pressure from other gas clouds pushes the gas inward.
Gravity pulls all the gas inward.
Pressure from light from nearby stars pushes the gas inward.
Opposite charges in the gas attract.
Some gas is sent outward, causing the rest to move inward to conserve momentum.
questions.why: Gravity pulls every bit of gas toward all the rest, so when a cloud is dense enough gravity makes it collapse and form a star and planets. A shock wave from a nearby supernova may start the collapse, but it is gravity that keeps it going. Pressure from light or other clouds, attraction of opposite charges (the gas is neutral overall) and momentum from outward-flung gas are not the main cause.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q4 (no printed key); key checked: gravity drives the collapse (supernova may trigger it): p. 220 (PDF p. 242); key 1 confirmed

questions.q: If an interstellar gas cloud shrinks in size, what does the law of conservation of energy predict it will do?
options: spin slower
heat up
spin faster
cool off
continue shrinking
questions.why: As the cloud shrinks, gravitational potential energy is converted into the kinetic energy of the falling gas. The particles collide and that motion becomes thermal energy, so the cloud heats up. Spinning faster is predicted by conservation of angular momentum, a different law. Cooling off or spinning slower is the opposite of what happens, and conservation of energy says nothing about it continuing to shrink.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q5 (no printed key); key checked: heating = conservation of energy: p. 220 (PDF p. 242); Ch8.2_pt1 slide 3; key 1 confirmed

questions.q: If an interstellar gas cloud shrinks in size, what does the law of conservation of angular momentum predict it will do?
options: cool off
continue shrinking
spin faster
heat up
spin slower
questions.why: A shrinking cloud has to spin faster to keep its angular momentum constant, just as a skater speeds up when she pulls in her arms. Heating up comes from conservation of energy, not angular momentum. Spinning slower would mean losing angular momentum, and cooling off or continuing to shrink are not predicted by this law.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q6 (no printed key); key checked: spin-up = conservation of angular momentum: p. 221 (PDF p. 243); Ch8.2_pt1 slide 2; key 2 confirmed

questions.q: According to our theory of solar system formation, why do all the planets orbit the Sun in the same direction and in nearly the same plane?
options: It is a coincidence, as we would expect that most other solar systems would not have all their planets orbiting in such a pattern.
Any planets that once orbited in the opposite direction or a different plane were ejected from the solar system.
The laws of conservation of energy and conservation of angular momentum ensure that any rotating, collapsing cloud will end up as a spinning disk.
The Sun formed first, and as it grew in size it spread into a disk, rather like the way a ball of dough can be flattened into a pizza by spinning it.
The original solar nebula happened to be disk shaped by chance.
questions.why: A collapsing, rotating cloud heats up, spins faster and has its random motions smoothed out by collisions, so it flattens into a disk turning in one direction. The planets formed in that disk, so they orbit in the same direction and nearly the same plane. This is a natural result, not a coincidence or a clean-up of misfits. The Sun formed at the centre of the disk; it did not form first and then spread out like pizza dough.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q7 (no printed key); key checked: heating, spinning, flattening: p. 220-221 (PDF p. 242-243); Ch8.2_pt1 slides 2-4; key 2 is the best available choice

questions.q: Which of the following lists the ingredients of the solar nebula from highest to lowest percentage of mass of the nebula?
options: hydrogen compounds, hydrogen and helium gas, metals, rocks
hydrogen compounds, rocks, metals, hydrogen and helium gas
hydrogen compounds, hydrogen and helium gas, rocks, metals
hydrogen and helium gas, hydrogen compounds, metals, rocks
hydrogen and helium gas, hydrogen compounds, rocks, metals
questions.why: By mass the solar nebula was about 98% hydrogen and helium gas, 1.4% hydrogen compounds (water, methane, ammonia), 0.4% rock and 0.2% metal. So the order from highest to lowest is hydrogen and helium gas, hydrogen compounds, rock, metal. The wrong lists put the gas lower or swap rock and metal with hydrogen compounds.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q8 (no printed key); key checked: Table 8.1: 98% H/He, 1.4% hydrogen compounds, 0.4% rock, 0.2% metal, p. 222 (PDF p. 244); key 4 confirmed

questions.q: About what percentage of the mass of the solar nebula consisted of elements other than hydrogen and helium?
options: 2 percent
0 percent
0.1 percent
80 percent
20 percent
questions.why: Hydrogen and helium made up about 98% of the nebula's mass, so everything else together (hydrogen compounds, rock and metal) was about 2%. Zero or 0.1% is too small to build the planets, and 20% or 80% would be far too much.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q9 (no printed key); key checked: about 98% hydrogen and helium, 2% everything else: p. 219 (PDF p. 241); key 0 confirmed

questions.q: The very first generation of star systems in the universe must have been born from gas that consisted entirely of hydrogen and helium (and no other elements). Which of the following statements is most likely to have been true about these first-generation star systems?
options: They did not have any planets or asteroids or comets.
They had terrestrial planets but no jovian planets.
They did not have any disks of gas around them as they formed.
They had asteroids and comets but no large planets.
questions.why: With only hydrogen and helium there is nothing that can condense into solid grains, so there would be no rock, metal or ice to build planetesimals. Without planetesimals there can be no asteroids or comets, and no planets either, because even gas giants grow from a solid core that then captures gas. Disks still form from any collapsing, spinning cloud, so the lack of a disk is not the answer.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q10 (no printed key); key checked: no heavy elements, no solids to condense: p. 219 (PDF p. 241, Think about it) and p. 222 (Table 8.1, PDF p. 244); key 0 confirmed

questions.q: What happened during the accretion phase of the early solar system?
options: Particles grew by colliding and sticking together.
Atoms of hydrogen and helium gas bonded together and solidified.
The solar nebula differentiated into metals inside of the frost line and ices beyond.
Earth gained its oceans from icy planetesimal capture.
Large planetesimals captured atmospheres from the solar nebula.
questions.why: Accretion is the growth of solid particles: tiny grains stuck together, then planetesimals grew and pulled in others by gravity. Separating metals and rocks inside the frost line from ices beyond it was condensation, which came before. Earth's water arrived later through impacts, and hydrogen and helium gas do not bond and solidify in the nebula.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q11 (no printed key); key checked: accretion = particles stick and grow: p. 223 (PDF p. 245); Ch8.2_pt1 slides 6-7; key 0 confirmed

questions.q: Which of the following accurately describes how the Jovian planetesimals were formed?
options: Planetesimals grew from tiny grains of rock and metal via static electricity and other non-gravitational forces. When they reached a critical size, they also began attracting hydrogen compounds and hydrogen and helium gas from the surrounding protoplanetary nebula.
Planetesimals grew from tiny grains of hydrogen compounds via gravity. When they reached a critical size, they also began attracting rocks and metals from the surrounding protoplanetary nebula.

Planetesimals grew from tiny grains of hydrogen compounds, rock, and metal via static electricity and other non-gravitational forces. When they reached a critical size, they also began attracting hydrogen and helium gas from the surrounding protoplanetary nebula via gravity.

Planetesimals grew from tiny grains of hydrogen compounds, rock, and metal via gravity. When they reached a critical size, they also began attracting hydrogen and helium gas from the surrounding protoplanetary nebula.
questions.why: Beyond the frost line the tiny grains were a mix of ice (hydrogen compounds), rock and metal. Gravity is much too weak to pull such small specks together, so they stuck by static electricity and other non-gravitational forces. Only when planetesimals were large enough did their gravity start to attract hydrogen and helium gas. The wrong options either start the process with gravity on tiny grains or leave out part of the mix of ice, rock and metal.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q12 (no printed key); key checked: tiny particles stick by electrostatic forces (p. 223, PDF p. 245), icy planetesimals then capture H/He by gravity (p. 224, PDF p. 246); Ch8.2_pt1 slide 8; key 2 confirmed

questions.q: How did most of the moons around Jovian planets come to be?
options: The Jovian moons are the scattered remnants of a fifth Jovian planet that was destroyed by an impact in the Heavy Bombardment, and which settled into orbit around the remaining Jovian planets.
Smaller planetesimals were gravitationally captured by the larger Jovian planetesimals and became the Jovian moons.
Parts of the Jovian planetesimals broke off in the accretion phase and became the Jovian moons.
They formed by accretion in much the same way that planets formed around the Sun in the protoplanetary nebula, but on a smaller scale.
questions.why: The large moons of the jovian planets formed in disks of gas and dust around each growing giant planet, by accretion in the same way planets formed around the Sun but on a smaller scale. That is why they orbit in the planet's rotation direction in nearly circular orbits. They did not come from a destroyed fifth planet or break off the planets. A few small odd moons were captured, but capture needs an object to lose energy (for example to friction in the planet's gas), so simple gravitational capture is not how most moons formed.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q13 (no printed key); key checked: moons formed in disks around jovian planets: p. 224 (PDF p. 246); Ch8.2_pt1 slide 9; captured moons only for small bodies p. 226 (PDF p. 248); key 3 confirmed

questions.q: The frost line of the solar system was located approximately between
options: the present-day orbits of Venus and Earth.
the present-day orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
the present-day orbits of Uranus and Neptune.
the present-day orbits of Mercury and Venus.
the Sun and the present-day orbit of Mercury.
questions.why: Hydrogen compounds freeze into ice only below about 150 K, and in the solar nebula that temperature was reached around 2.7 AU, which is between the present orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Between Mercury and Earth the nebula was too hot for ice, and the orbits of Uranus and Neptune are far beyond the frost line.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q14 (no printed key); key checked: frost line between Mars and Jupiter, about 2.7 AU: p. 223 (PDF p. 245); key 1 confirmed

questions.q: Why are the inner planets made of denser materials than the outer planets?
options: In the inner part of the nebula only metals and rocks were able to condense because of the high temperatures, whereas hydrogen compounds, although more abundant, were only able to condense in the cooler outer regions.

When the solar nebula formed a disk, materials naturally segregated into bands, and in our particular solar system, the denser materials settled nearer the Sun, while lighter materials are found in the outer part.
The Sun's gravity pulled denser materials toward the inner part of the solar nebula, while lighter gases escaped more easily.
In the beginning, when the protoplanetary disk was spinning faster, centrifugal forces flung the lighter materials toward the outer parts of the solar nebula.
Denser materials were heavier and sank to the center of the nebula.
questions.why: Near the young Sun, ices such as water could not stay frozen, so the only solids available there were metal and rock, even though ice-forming material was more plentiful overall. Beyond the frost line ices could condense as well, so the outer planets gained lighter, icy material and far more of it. The Sun's gravity pulling dense material in, spinning flinging light material out, or dense material sinking are not what happened, because every ingredient orbits the Sun in the same way regardless of its density.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q15 (no printed key); key checked: temperature, not Sun's gravity, caused the compositional split: p. 223 and Common Misconceptions box (PDF p. 245); Ch8.2_pt1 slide 5; key 0 confirmed

questions.q: The nebular theory predicts that the young Sun should have been rotating quite rapidly, but the Sun rotates slowly today. Can this fact be explained by the nebular theory?
options: Yes, objects always slow their rotations over time.
Yes; the young Sun's solar wind would have carried away angular momentum, slowing the Sun's rotation.
No, it is a complete mystery as to why the Sun would rotate slowly today.
questions.why: Yes. The young Sun spun fast and had a strong magnetic field and wind. Its field dragged on the charged particles in the surrounding gas, transferring angular momentum to them, and the wind and radiation carried that gas and its angular momentum away into space, slowing the Sun. Objects do not always slow down, because angular momentum is conserved unless it is transferred elsewhere. It is not a mystery.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q16 (no printed key); key checked: Sun's magnetic field dragged on charged particles in the nebula; wind and cleared gas carried angular momentum away: p. 225 (PDF p. 247); Ch8.2_pt2 slide 1; key 1 confirmed

questions.q: Hydrogen compounds in the solar nebula could condense into ice at temperatures of about 150 K. Suppose they instead could have condensed only at temperatures below 50 K? What would have been different in the solar nebula?
options: Jovian planets would have formed inside the frost line.
The frost line would have been farther from the Sun.
The frost line would have been closer to the Sun.
Terrestrial planets would have formed outside the frost line.
questions.why: Ice can form only where the gas is colder than the temperature at which the compound condenses. If hydrogen compounds needed to be below 50 K instead of 150 K, the nebula would have to be much colder, which happens only farther from the Sun, so the frost line would be farther out. Terrestrial planets form inside the frost line and jovian planets outside it, so those other statements contradict the definition.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q17 (no printed key); key checked: lower condensation temperature puts the frost line farther out: p. 222-223 (PDF p. 244-245); key 1 confirmed

questions.q: Observations of young stars suggest that when the Sun was young, the solar wind
options: was weaker than it is today.
was stronger than it is today.
was about the same strength as it is today.
was nonexistent.
blew outward only along the Sun's poles.
questions.why: Young stars rotate fast and have strong magnetic fields, so they have much stronger winds and emit more high-energy radiation than older stars. The young Sun's strong wind and radiation helped blow away the leftover gas of the solar nebula. So it was stronger than today, not weaker, the same or absent, and the wind blew in all directions.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q18 (no printed key); key checked: young stars have much stronger winds: p. 224 (PDF p. 246); key 1 confirmed

questions.q: What might have happened if the hydrogen and helium gas pervading the early Solar System had not been driven out (i.e., if the solar nebula had not been cleared)?
options: The asteroids would have been able to assemble into a planet.
Accretion would have been stifled, leading to much smaller planets.
Only the Jovian planets would have grown much larger.
All planets would have grown much larger, and the terrestrial planets would have accreted hydrogen and helium gas.
questions.why: If the hydrogen and helium had stayed, the nebula would have kept cooling until ices could form even in the inner Solar System, so the terrestrial planets could have grown larger and could have gathered hydrogen and helium gas, changing their basic nature. Asteroids do not assemble into a planet because the gas is cleared, and gas would not stifle growth or make only the jovian planets larger.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q19 (no printed key); key checked: if the gas had stayed, terrestrial planets might have accreted ices and perhaps H/He: p. 224 (PDF p. 246); key 3 confirmed

questions.q: According to the nebular theory, what are asteroids and comets?
options: leftover planetesimals that never accreted into planets
chunks of rock or ice that condensed long after the planets had formed
the shattered remains of collisions between planets
the shattered remains of collisions between moons
chunks of rock or ice that have been expelled from the planets by volcanoes
questions.why: Asteroids (rocky, from inside the frost line) and comets (icy, from beyond it) are leftover planetesimals that never became part of a planet. They did not form long after the planets, are not the remains of collisions between planets or moons, and are not volcanic debris.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q20 (no printed key); key checked: asteroids and comets are leftover planetesimals: p. 225 (PDF p. 247); Ch8.2_pt2 slide 2; key 0 confirmed

questions.q: What happened during the heavy bombardment?
options: Planetesimals collided with one another and stuck together to form planets.
A supernova disrupted a gas cloud, causing it to start collapsing to form the solar system.
The planets of the solar system suffered many impacts.
A large meteor collided with Earth, killing the dinosaurs.
The planets collided with one another.
questions.why: Once the planets had formed, the leftover planetesimals kept slamming into them and their moons for a few hundred million years; this cratering era is the heavy bombardment. Planetesimals sticking together to form planets was accretion, which came earlier. A supernova may have triggered the nebula's collapse, the dinosaur impact happened about 66 million years ago, and the planets did not collide with each other.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q21 (no printed key); key checked: heavy bombardment lasted a few hundred million years: p. 226 (PDF p. 248); Ch8.2_pt2 slide 3; key 2 confirmed

questions.q: What is the giant impact hypothesis for the origin of the Moon?
options: The Moon formed just like Earth, from accretion in the solar nebula.
The Moon formed from material blasted out of Earth's mantle and crust by the impact of a Mars-size object.
The Moon formed when two gigantic asteroids collided with one another.
The Moon originally was about the same size as Earth, but a giant impact blasted most of it away so that it ended up much smaller than Earth.
questions.why: The giant impact hypothesis says a Mars-size object hit the young Earth, blasting material from Earth's outer rocky layers into orbit, where it gathered to form the Moon. The Moon did not form in the nebula like Earth, because its density and composition differ. It did not come from two asteroids colliding, and it was not once an Earth-sized body that lost most of its mass.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q22 (no printed key); key checked: giant impact hypothesis: p. 227 (PDF p. 249); key 1 confirmed

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT directly support the giant impact hypothesis for the formation of our Moon?
options: The Moon is very quiet geologically compared to most other bodies.
The Moon lacks volatile chemicals that would vaporize in a large impact.
The Moon is very large for its host body, the Earth.
Computer simulations show that a collision between planetesimals can result in an Earth-Moon system like ours.
questions.why: The Moon's lack of volcanism and tectonics is only a result of its small size, which let it cool quickly, and it says nothing about how the Moon formed. The other three do support the hypothesis: the missing volatile chemicals fit the heat of an impact vaporizing them, computer simulations can reproduce the Earth-Moon system, and the Moon's large size relative to Earth is what the impact idea explains and what capture cannot.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q23 (no printed key); key checked: evidence for the giant impact: simulations, similar outer layers, missing volatiles (Ch8.2_pt2 slide 7; p. 227, PDF p. 249); the Moon's geological quiet is not on that list and is unrelated to its origin; key 0 kept, fairly confident (the Moon's large size is the puzzle the impact explains, p. 227)

questions.q: We know that Earth has water. However, according to our theory of solar system formation, the inner solar system was too hot for hydrogen compounds like water to condense. What do we conclude?
options: Earth's water likely was brought here by asteroids or comets that formed beyond the frost line.
Our theory of solar system formation will need modification because it is unable to account for the existence of water on Earth.
Water arrived on Earth at a time when it rained throughout the inner solar system.
Earth's water probably originated through chemical reactions among the rock and metal of Earth's interior.
questions.why: The terrestrial planets formed where it was too hot for ice, so Earth's water was probably delivered by icy planetesimals, asteroids or comets that formed beyond the frost line and struck Earth during the heavy bombardment. The theory is therefore not broken by Earth's water. It did not rain throughout the inner nebula, and water does not come from chemical reactions of rock and metal alone.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q24 (no printed key); key checked: water brought by icy planetesimals from beyond the frost line: p. 226 (PDF p. 248); Ch8.2_pt2 slide 4; key 0 confirmed

questions.q: According to our theory of solar system formation, why do we find some exceptions to the general rules and patterns of the planets?
options: The exceptions are probably the result of the Sun passing very close to another star billions of years ago.
The exceptions probably represent objects that formed recently, rather than early in the history of the solar system.
The exceptions probably represent objects that were captured by our solar system from interstellar space.
Most of the exceptions are the result of giant impacts or close gravitational encounters.
Our theory is not quite correct because it cannot explain these exceptions.
questions.why: The nebular theory explains the general patterns with the collapse of the nebula, and it explains most exceptions, such as Uranus's tilt, Venus's backward spin and Earth's large Moon, by random events like giant impacts and close gravitational encounters among leftover planetesimals. A star passing close to the Sun is the discarded close encounter hypothesis. The exceptions are not recent objects, captured moons were mostly captured from material orbiting the Sun rather than interstellar space, and exceptions do not show the theory is wrong.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q25 (no printed key); key checked: exceptions arise from collisions or close gravitational encounters: p. 226 (PDF p. 248); Ch8.2_pt2 slide 5; key 3 confirmed

questions.q: Suppose the Sun had been born with more mass, making it larger and hotter. Which of the following consequences would we expect according to the nebular theory?
options: Jovian planets would have formed farther from the Sun.
Asteroids would have formed closer to the Sun.
There would be no comets.
There would have been no solar nebula in which material could condense to form planets.
questions.why: A more massive, hotter Sun would heat the nebula more, so the temperature low enough for ices to form would be reached farther from the Sun, and the frost line, where jovian planets form, would be farther out. Asteroids, which form inside the frost line, would also form farther out, not closer. Comets would still form, and a nebula would still exist.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q26 (no printed key); key checked: hotter Sun moves the frost line out: p. 223 (PDF p. 245); key 0 confirmed

questions.q: The lithosphere of a planet is the layer that consists of
options: material between the crust and the mantle.
the rigid rocky material of the crust and uppermost portion of the mantle.
material above the crust.
the lava that comes out of volcanoes.
the softer rocky material of the mantle.
questions.why: Think of the lithosphere as a planet's stiff outer shell: the crust together with the cold top layer of the mantle beneath it. What sets the boundary is how stiff the rock is, not what chemicals it contains. The softer rock below it is the asthenosphere, the crust is only part of the lithosphere, and lava is just molten rock that erupts.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q27 (no printed key); key checked: lithosphere = crust plus uppermost mantle, rigid: p. 240 (PDF p. 262); Ch9.1_pt1 slide 9; key 1 confirmed

questions.q: How do scientists learn about the internal composition of our planet?
options: They collect seismic data to infer the densities and thicknesses of different regions in the Earth's interior.
They use x-ray and gamma ray imaging, which can penetrate the Earth's surface.
They drill into the earth with state-of-the-art equipment to collect samples from deep within the Earth's interior.
They drop special, heat-resistant probes into volcanoes to explore and obtain data from underneath the Earth's crust.
questions.why: We cannot drill deep or see inside, so scientists use seismic waves from earthquakes. Their speeds and paths depend on density and on whether the material is solid or liquid, which reveals the layers inside Earth. X-rays and gamma rays do not penetrate far, drills reach less than 1% of the way to the centre, and probes cannot be dropped into volcanoes that deep.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q28 (no printed key); key checked: seismic waves: p. 239 and Special Topic p. 241 (PDF p. 261, 263); Ch9.1_pt1 slides 4-5; key 0 confirmed

questions.q: Which of the following best describes differentiation in planetary geology?
options: One planet's surface evolves differently from another planet's surface.
Different types of minerals form a conglomerate rock.
Gravity separates molten materials according to density.
One part of a planet's surface evolves differently from another part of the same planet's surface.
Dense materials condense at higher temperatures than less dense materials.
questions.why: Differentiation happens when a planet is molten enough that gravity separates material by density: dense metals sink to the core and lighter rock rises to form the mantle and crust, like oil and water separating. The other options mix this up with how surfaces evolve, how rocks form or how materials condense.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q29 (no printed key); key checked: differentiation: p. 239 (PDF p. 261); Ch9.1_pt2 slide 1; key 2 confirmed

questions.q: Which internal energy source is the most important in continuing to heat the terrestrial planets today?
options: accretion
differentiation
tidal heating
radioactivity
questions.why: Heat from accretion and differentiation was mostly deposited when the planets were young, while radioactive decay of uranium, potassium and thorium is still releasing heat, so it is the main source now. Tidal heating matters for moons such as Io, but not for the terrestrial planets.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q30 (no printed key); key checked: radioactive decay is the only major heat source today: p. 242 (PDF p. 264); Ch9.1_pt2 slide 3; key 3 confirmed

questions.q: Which of the following best describes convection?
options: Warm material expands and rises while cool material contracts and falls.
Bubbles of gas move upward through a liquid of the same temperature.
A liquid separates according to density, such as oil and water separating in a jar.
Rocks sink in water.
Warm material gets even warmer and cool material gets even cooler.
questions.why: Convection is the process in which warm material expands and rises while cooler material contracts and falls, carrying heat upward, as in a pot of soup or in Earth's mantle. Gas bubbles rising, a liquid separating by density and rocks sinking in water are other ideas, and in convection warm material does not simply warm up more.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q31 (no printed key); key checked: convection: p. 242 (PDF p. 264); Ch9.1_pt2 slide 4; key 0 confirmed

questions.q: What are the three main sources of internal heat for terrestrial planets?
options: convection, differentiation, and eruption
conduction, differentiation, and accretion
accretion, differentiation, and eruption
conduction, convection, and eruption
accretion, differentiation, and radioactivity
questions.why: Terrestrial planets get internal heat from accretion (impacts of planetesimals), differentiation (dense material sinking) and radioactive decay. Convection, conduction and eruption are ways heat moves or escapes, not sources of heat.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q32 (no printed key); key checked: accretion, differentiation, radioactive decay: p. 241 (PDF p. 263); Ch9.1_pt2 slide 2; key 4 confirmed

questions.q: What conditions are thought to be necessary for a terrestrial planet to have a strong magnetic field?
options: fast rotation only
both a metal core and a rocky mantle
a molten metallic core only
a rocky mantle only
both a molten metallic core and reasonably fast rotation
questions.why: A strong magnetic field needs an electrically conducting fluid such as molten metal, convection in it, and reasonably fast rotation. Earth has a molten outer core and rotates in a day, so it has a strong field. A molten core alone is not enough (Venus rotates very slowly), fast rotation alone is not enough, and a metal core with a rocky mantle can be solid, as with the Moon and Mars.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q33 (no printed key); key checked: molten conducting interior, convection, moderately rapid rotation: p. 244 (PDF p. 266); Ch9.1_pt2 slide 9; key 4 is the best available choice

questions.q: What is the main process by which heat flows upward through the lithosphere?
options: conduction
differentiation
convection
radiation
accretion
questions.why: Inside the rigid lithosphere the rock cannot flow, so mantle convection stops at its base and heat moves upward mainly by conduction, atom to atom through contact, and is then radiated into space. Differentiation and accretion are heat sources, convection occurs below the lithosphere, and radiation is how the heat leaves from the surface into space.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q34 (no printed key); key checked: heat moves up through the lithosphere mainly by conduction: p. 243 (PDF p. 265) and Fig. 9.5; key 0 confirmed

questions.q: If a spherical body has a surface area of 36π km², what is its volume? (Recall that the surface area-to-volume ratio of a sphere is 3/r.)
options: 216 km³
36π km³
10π km³
3 km³
questions.why: A sphere's surface area is 4πr². If 4πr² = 36π, then r² = 9 and r = 3 km. The surface area to volume ratio is 3/r = 1 per km, so volume = surface area ÷ ratio = 36π km² ÷ (1 per km) = 36π km³. Check: (4/3)π(3)³ = 36π km³. The 216 km³ choice cubes the diameter (6³) instead of using (4/3)πr³, and 3 km³ is just the number 3/r, not a volume.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q35 (no printed key); key checked: numbers lost in the student's paste; reconstructed with surface area 36 pi km^2 (r = 3 km, V = 36 pi km^3, the only value of the surface area that lands on one of the four given options); Ch9.1_pt2 slide 6; p. 243 Mathematical Insight 9.1 (PDF p. 265); key 1

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an effect of a planet having a larger size?
options: The planet undergoes internal geological activity for longer.
The planet retains an atmosphere for longer and experiences more erosion.
The planet has a warmer surface temperature.
The planet loses heat less quickly.
questions.why: A larger planet keeps its interior heat longer, so it stays geologically active longer, and its stronger gravity holds an atmosphere longer, leading to more erosion. Surface temperature is not an effect of size, because it depends mainly on distance from the Sun and on the atmosphere. Earth and Venus are almost the same size but have very different surface temperatures.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q36 (no printed key); key checked: larger worlds stay active longer and keep an atmosphere; temperature depends on distance from the Sun: Ch9.2 slides 21-22; p. 243 (PDF p. 265); key 2 confirmed

questions.q: Which terrestrial world has the strongest magnetic field?
options: the Moon
Venus
Mars
Mercury
Earth
questions.why: Earth has a molten, convecting metal outer core and rotates fairly quickly, so it has a strong global magnetic field. The Moon and Mars have cooled too much to have such a core, Venus rotates too slowly, and Mercury has only a weak field.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q37 (no printed key); key checked: Earth has the strongest field of the terrestrial worlds: p. 244 (PDF p. 266); Ch9.1_pt2 slide 10; key 4 confirmed

questions.q: Approximately how large (across) is an impact crater compared to the size of the impactor?
options: 10 times larger
100 times larger
the same size
1000 times larger
10—20 percent larger
questions.why: Because the impactor explodes on contact and blasts out material all around, the crater ends up roughly ten times wider than the object that hit. For example, a 1 km asteroid makes a crater about 10 km across. The other sizes are too large or too small.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q38 (no printed key); key checked: craters about 10 times as wide as the impactor: p. 245 (PDF p. 267); Ch9.2 slide 3; key 0 confirmed

questions.q: Which factor below determines the steepness of a volcano?
options: the duration of the eruption
the age of the volcano
the temperature of the lava
the volume of lava
how easily the lava flows
questions.why: Thick, sticky lava cannot flow far, so it piles up into steep stratovolcanoes, while runny lava spreads out into gently sloping shield volcanoes or flat lava plains. Steepness is set by how easily the lava flows (its viscosity), not by how long the volcano erupted, its age or the total volume of lava.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q39 (no printed key); key checked: thicker lava makes steeper volcanoes: p. 246 (PDF p. 268); Ch9.2 slide 9; key 4 confirmed

questions.q: A planet is most likely to have volcanic and tectonic activity if it has
options: low internal temperature.
high internal temperature.
high surface gravity.
low surface gravity.
a dense atmosphere.
questions.why: Volcanism and tectonics are driven by internal heat, which melts rock and drives mantle convection. So a planet with a high internal temperature is most likely to be active. A low internal temperature leads to a geologically dead planet, and surface gravity or a thick atmosphere does not drive volcanism.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q40 (no printed key); key checked: geological activity is driven by internal heat: p. 241 (PDF p. 263); key 1 confirmed

questions.q: What can we conclude when we see a region of a planet that is not as heavily cratered as other regions?
options: There is little volcanic activity to create craters.
The surface in the region is younger than the surface in more heavily cratered regions.
The planet is rotating very slowly and only one side was hit by impactors.
The surface in the region is older than the surface in more heavily cratered regions.
The planet formed after the age of bombardment and missed out on getting hit by leftover planetesimals.
questions.why: Craters build up over time, so a region with fewer craters must have been resurfaced more recently, for example by lava or erosion, which erased older craters. That makes it younger than a heavily cratered region. Volcanic activity erases craters rather than makes them, and planets do not get impacts on only one side.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q41 (no printed key); key checked: fewer craters means a younger surface: p. 248 (PDF p. 270); Ch9.2 slides 5-6; key 1 confirmed

questions.q: Which of the following natural geological features is NOT a result of erosion?
options: Sand dunes
Canyons
Fjords
Rift valleys
River deltas
questions.why: Rift valleys form when tectonic forces pull the crust apart, not by erosion. Canyons are cut by rivers, fjords are valleys carved by glaciers, sand dunes are shaped by wind and river deltas are built from sediment carried by water, so all of these come from erosion.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q42 (no printed key); key checked: erosion features vs tectonic rifts: p. 248 (PDF p. 270, Fig. 9.14); p. 268 (PDF p. 290, rift valleys); Ch9.2 slides 16-20, 25; key 3 confirmed

questions.q: Why is seafloor crust generally much younger than continental crust?
options: Seafloor crust is closer to Earth's mantle than continental crust, so it is heated more and experiences convection that continuously replaces older crust.
Seafloor crust is thinner and denser, so it gets pushed beneath the continental crust wherever they meet and is constantly recycled this way.
The seafloor experiences continuous erosion by the ocean, exposing new crust, but the rocks on land erode much more slowly.
questions.why: Seafloor crust is thin and dense, so where it meets thicker, lighter continental crust it is pushed down in a subduction zone and recycled into the mantle. That is why seafloor crust is usually less than about 200 million years old, while continental crust can be billions of years old. It is not closer to the mantle and replaced by convection, and ocean water erodes the seafloor very little.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q43 (no printed key); key checked: seafloor crust is thinner, denser and younger and is recycled by subduction: p. 265-266 (PDF p. 287-288); Ch9.6 slides 6-7; key 1 confirmed

questions.q: What is the overall geological process occurring at the Great Rift Valley in Africa?
options: Continental crust is pushing together at a convergent plate boundary.
Ocean crust is subducting under continental crust.
Continental crust is being pulled apart at a divergent plate boundary.
Two tectonic plates are sliding past each other, resulting in earthquakes.
questions.why: The Great Rift Valley in East Africa is where continental crust is being pulled apart at a divergent boundary, thinning the crust so a rift valley forms, and eventually the continent could split. Convergent boundaries push together, subduction is an ocean plate going under another plate, and sliding past is a transform fault like the San Andreas.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q44 (no printed key); key checked: East African rift: continental plates pulling apart: p. 268 (PDF p. 290); Ch9.6 slide 9; key 2 confirmed

questions.q: What process has played the greatest role in determining the arrangement of the continents on Earth?
options: impact cratering
acid rain
erosion
volcanism
plate tectonics
questions.why: The slow movement of tectonic plates over millions of years has carried the continents into their present arrangement. Impacts, acid rain, erosion and volcanism shape surfaces but do not move continents.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q45 (no printed key); key checked: Earth is shaped primarily by plate tectonics: p. 264 (PDF p. 286); key 4 confirmed

questions.q: On average, approximately how fast do plates move with plate tectonics on Earth?
options: They do not move at all, except during earthquakes.
a few centimeters per year
a few millimeters per century
a few centimeters per century
a few kilometers per hour
questions.why: Tectonic plates move a few centimeters per year, about as fast as fingernails grow. That is slow, but over millions of years it moves continents thousands of kilometers. Plates are not stationary except in earthquakes, and a few millimeters per century or a few centimeters per century are far too slow, while a few kilometers per hour is much too fast.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q46 (no printed key); key checked: plates move a few centimeters per year: p. 265 (PDF p. 287); Ch9.6 slides 4 and 12; key 1 confirmed

questions.q: Deep trenches in the ocean mark places where
options: one plate moves under another, returning older crust to the mantle.
plates pull apart, leaving great rifts in the crust.
plates push together, creating ocean mountain chains.
hot mantle material rises upward and spreads sideways, pushing the plates apart.
plates slip sideways relative to one another.
questions.why: Deep ocean trenches mark subduction zones, where the denser plate of seafloor crust moves under another plate and is returned to the mantle. Plates pulling apart make rifts and mid-ocean ridges, plates pushing together can make mountains, and plates sliding sideways make faults.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q47 (no printed key); key checked: ocean trenches form at subduction zones: p. 266 (PDF p. 288) and Fig. 9.44; Ch9.6 slide 7 (note: Ch9.6 slide 13 loosely says trenches form at divergent boundaries, which conflicts with the book; the book is explicit); key 0 confirmed

questions.q: The islands of Hawaii were created by
options: a plate that has run up against an existing continental plate.
a fault.
plumes of hot mantle rising in a hot spot within a plate.
plates that have slipped sideways relative to each other, creating a fault.
thin continental crust separating and creating a rift valley.
questions.why: The Hawaiian Islands formed over a hot spot, a plume of hot mantle rising inside the Pacific plate. As the plate moves over the hot spot, new volcanoes build islands in a chain. Hawaii is not on a plate boundary, so a fault, a collision or a rift valley is not the cause.
questions.source: admin-only: student's solar system formation and planetary geology set Q48 (no printed key); key checked: Hawaii formed over a mantle hot spot: p. 268 (PDF p. 290); Ch9.6 slide 11; key 2 confirmed

tests.title: Practice Test 3: Telescopes to Planetary Geology
tests.blurb: 24 questions on lenses and telescopes, solar system patterns, how the solar system formed, and planetary interiors and surfaces.

questions.q: How does a lens work?
options: It speeds up light traveling through it, delivering more power to the resulting image, which is focused at the focal plane.
It refracts light rays in a manner that renders a coherent image on the image plane.
It reflects light rays in a manner that renders a coherent image at the focal point.
It uses diffraction to separate wavelengths, forming a coherent image on the image plane.
It forces light to travel through a narrow opening, decreasing circles of confusion and resulting in a coherent image on the focal plane.
questions.why: A lens bends (refracts) light so that rays from each point of the object meet at one point on the image plane, giving a coherent image. Mirrors reflect; a pinhole uses a narrow opening; light actually slows down in glass.

questions.q: Suppose a 40-meter radio dish is used to observe radio light from a galaxy with a wavelength of 1 meter. Meanwhile, a 10-meter telescope observes infrared light from the same galaxy with a wavelength of 1 micron (10^-6 m). Which statement is true?
options: The radio telescope has 4 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is greater, rendering the radio image less sharp.
The radio telescope has 16 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is smaller, rendering the radio image less sharp.
The radio telescope has 16 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is greater, rendering the radio image less sharp.
The radio telescope has 4 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is smaller, rendering the radio image sharper.
The radio telescope has 16 times the light-collecting area of the infrared telescope and its minimum angular resolution is greater, rendering the radio image sharper.
questions.why: Area grows as D squared: (40/10)^2 = 16 times. Smallest resolvable angle goes as wavelength/D: radio 1/40 = 0.025 versus infrared 10^-6/10 = 10^-7. The radio angle is far larger, so its image is less sharp.

questions.q: Which of the following steps would NOT help to reduce or eliminate atmospheric distortions that interfere with telescope observations?
options: Putting a telescope in space to bypass the atmosphere.
Waiting for a break in the weather.
Using adaptive optics to account for distortions in real time.
Operating a telescope in a better location with drier air and a higher altitude.
Using interferometry to achieve a better angular resolution across multiple telescopes.
questions.why: Interferometry links telescopes to act like one very wide dish, improving resolution, but it does nothing about the air bending the light. Space, adaptive optics, high dry sites and clear (calm) skies all reduce what the atmosphere does to the light.

questions.q: Which of the following wavelength ranges is it best to put a telescope into space to detect?
options: Radio waves
X-rays
Visible
Infrared
None of the above require space telescopes to detect.
questions.why: The atmosphere absorbs X-rays completely, so X-ray telescopes must be above it. Radio and visible light reach the ground, and much infrared work can be done from high, dry mountains.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an exception to the general patterns in the Solar System? (An exception is a feature that would likely not be present if a random or catastrophic event had not occurred.)
options: the retrograde rotation of Venus
the large size of the Moon compared to the Earth
the extensive ring system of Saturn
the extreme obliquity of Uranus
the backwards orbit of Triton around Neptune
questions.why: All the jovian planets have rings, so Saturn's rings fit the normal pattern. Venus spinning backwards, Uranus's huge tilt, Earth's oversized Moon and Triton's backwards orbit are the classic exceptions, probably caused by impacts or captures.

questions.q: Which of the following tasks is an orbiter mission generally better suited for than a lander mission?
options: High-detail local topographical mapping
Sample collection
Conducting chemical tests of the surface
Seismological tests
Magnetosphere measurement
questions.why: A planet's magnetosphere surrounds the whole world, so a spacecraft moving through it in orbit measures it best. Sampling, surface chemistry, seismometers and close-up local mapping need a lander or rover on the ground.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a true difference between Earth and Venus?
options: Earth has frozen water, but Venus does not.
Earth has a strong magnetic field, but Venus does not.
Earth has tectonics, but Venus does not.
Earth experiences large-scale erosion, but Venus does not.
Earth's surface can be seen from space with the human eye, but Venus' surface cannot.
questions.why: Venus does have tectonics: its surface is folded and cracked by forces from its hot interior. What it lacks is plate tectonics. The other statements are true differences.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a true difference between Saturn and Uranus?
options: Saturn has rings but Uranus does not.
Saturn is much larger and more massive than Uranus.
Saturn is less dense than Uranus.
Uranus is chemically more complex than Saturn.
Uranus has a much longer year than Saturn.
questions.why: Uranus has rings too (all four jovian planets do), so this is not a real difference. Saturn is bigger and less dense; Uranus has more hydrogen compounds and an 84-year orbit versus Saturn's 29 years.

questions.q: Where are most comets in the Solar System found?
options: beyond the frost line between Jupiter and Neptune
between the Sun and Earth
between Mars and Jupiter
beyond Neptune in the Oort cloud
beyond Neptune in the Kuiper belt
questions.why: The Oort cloud, a huge sphere far beyond Neptune, holds possibly trillions of comets, far more than the Kuiper belt. The region between Mars and Jupiter is the asteroid belt.

questions.q: Where can we find the BEST observational evidence of our current theory of Solar System formation?
options: In the spectra of stars.
In the dark matter halos of distant galaxies.
In nearby nebulae.
In the Kuiper belt and Oort cloud.
In supernova explosions of nearby stars.
questions.why: In nearby clouds of gas we can watch stars forming right now, surrounded by flattened spinning disks of gas and dust, just as the nebular theory predicts for our own Sun.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence of energy conversion processes that occurred in the formation of the early Solar System?
options: Heat energy was converted into gravitational potential energy as the solar nebula collapsed to form the Sun, and some of this potential energy was then converted into nuclear energy to kickstart the Sun's fusion reactions.
Gravitational potential energy was converted into kinetic energy as the nebula collapsed, and most of this energy was dissipated as heat and radiation.
Kinetic energy was converted into gravitational potential energy as the nebula collapsed, and this potential energy caused the Sun to shrink and spin faster.

Gravitational potential energy was converted to kinetic energy as the nebula collapsed, and most of this energy was converted into chemical energy to create the raw materials from which the planets could form.
Kinetic energy was converted into nuclear energy as the Sun formed, and some of this nuclear energy was converted into radiation to generate the solar wind.
questions.why: As the cloud fell inward, gravitational potential energy became the motion (kinetic energy) of its particles. Collisions turned that motion into heat, and much of the heat escaped as radiation.

questions.q: Why are the Jovian planets so much larger than the terrestrial planets?
options: The Jovian planetesimals formed earlier in the Solar System's history, allowing them to accrete more material than the terrestrial planets.
The Jovian planetesimals were cooler than the terrestrial ones, and could accrete hydrogen and helium gas onto them through condensation.
The Jovian planetesimals formed beyond the frost line for hydrogen and helium, which allowed them to capture these gases and grow larger than the terrestrial ones.

The Jovian planetesimals grew more quickly than the terrestrial ones since they could incorporate hydrogen compounds, and were thus able to capture large amounts of hydrogen and helium gas before it was cleared out by the solar wind.
The Jovian planetesimals simply had more material to assemble from, as their orbits were larger.
questions.why: Beyond the frost line, ices of hydrogen compounds (water, methane, ammonia) could condense, so planetesimals there had far more solid material and grew big fast. Their strong gravity then pulled in hydrogen and helium gas before the young Sun's wind cleared it. The frost line is for hydrogen compounds, not hydrogen and helium, which never condense.

questions.q: Which of the following statements best explains why all the major planets orbit the Sun in the same direction and in nearly the same plane?
options: The Sun's gravity is strongest at its equator, so it pulled all the planets into this orbital alignment.
The planets that did not orbit in the same direction and in different planes got destroyed by collisions or were flung out of the Solar System by gravity.
The Sun's rotation spun out the planets as it formed.
The planets originally orbited in different directions, but gravity later pulled them into an ordered formation.
The planets formed from a disk of rotating gas, and their orbits therefore match the direction and plane of the disk's rotation.
questions.why: The collapsing nebula spun faster and flattened into a disk. Planets that grew within that spinning disk inherited its direction and its plane.

questions.q: What is the correct timeline for the formation of the Solar System? (Hint: remember how long the heavy bombardment took, and what would have happened if the solar nebula had not been cleared fairly quickly.)
options: The solar nebula collapsed, the solar nebula was cleared, the planetesimals grew via accretion, the heavy bombardment ended.
The solar nebula collapsed, the planetesimals grew via accretion, the heavy bombardment ended, the solar nebula was cleared.
The solar nebula collapsed, the heavy bombardment ended, the planetesimals grew via accretion, the solar nebula was cleared.
The solar nebula collapsed, the solar nebula was cleared, the heavy bombardment ended, the planetesimals grew via accretion.
The solar nebula collapsed, the planetesimals grew via accretion, the solar nebula was cleared, the heavy bombardment ended.
questions.why: Collapse came first, then planetesimals grew by accretion. The leftover gas was cleared early (otherwise the terrestrial planets would have kept gathering gas), and the heavy bombardment dragged on for a few hundred million years after that.

questions.q: Which of the following did NOT happen during the heavy bombardment?
options: The Moon formed.
Earth acquired its water and life began to develop.
Planetesimals were flung by gravitational encounters in different directions, some becoming the moons of larger planetesimals.
The Sun formed at its current location and hydrogen fusion began.
Some planetesimals collided violently, resulting in unusual tilts or rotation directions.
questions.why: The Sun formed and began fusion at the very start, when the centre of the collapsing nebula grew hot and dense, long before the bombardment by leftover planetesimals.

questions.q: Which of the following properties is MOST important in determining the boundary between the lithosphere and the asthenosphere of the Earth?
options: rock strength and temperature
chemical composition
density
physical state (liquid, solid)
geological age
questions.why: The lithosphere is cool, rigid rock; the asthenosphere below is warmer, softer rock that can flow slowly. Both are solid and similar in makeup, so the boundary is set by temperature and strength.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the heating of Earth's interior is NOT true?
options: Radioactivity is the dominant source of internal heating today.
Impacts during accretion and the heavy bombardment released enormous quantities of heat in the past, but this heat has since completely dissipated.
Differentiation was once a major heat source, but no longer contributes much to Earth's internal heat budget.
Convection does not produce any heat within Earth's interior.
Eventually, all radioactive elements on Earth will decay, differentiation will cease, and all internal heat sources will be exhausted, rendering Earth geologically dead.
questions.why: Heat from accretion has not completely escaped: a large planet like Earth keeps part of its early heat for billions of years, which is one reason it is still active. Radioactive decay is the main heat source today, and convection only moves heat, it does not make it.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding differentiation and convection in geology is TRUE?
options: Differentiation only involves material sinking, but convection involves material both rising and sinking.
Differentiation occurs throughout the interior of a planet, but convection takes place only in the core.
Differentiation involves rocks and metals, but convection involves magma (liquid rock).
Differentiation concluded long ago, but convection continues to this day.
Differentiation involves the large-scale movement of material, but convection is a microscopic heat transport process.
questions.why: Differentiation (dense metal sinking to the core, lighter rock rising) happened early in Earth's history. Mantle convection, slow flow of hot solid rock, still goes on today. Light material also rises during differentiation, and convection is large scale and mostly in solid rock.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes why Mercury does NOT have a strong magnetic field?
options: Mercury has a large iron core relative to its size.
Mercury has a very long day.
Mercury is too close to the Sun, leading to the erosion of its magnetic field by the solar wind.
Mercury has very little atmosphere.
Mercury's temperature gradient interferes with the generation of a strong magnetic field.
questions.why: A strong magnetic field needs a convecting, electrically conducting core and fairly rapid rotation. Mercury rotates very slowly (its day lasts months), so its field is weak despite its large iron core.

questions.q: Jupiter's moon Callisto has many more craters on its surface than either Io or Europa. What can we conclude from this?
options: Callisto has been struck by many more impactors than Io or Europa.
Callisto's surface is much younger, likely because geological processes on Io and Europa have had time to erode those moons' craters.
Callisto's surface is much older, likely because geological processes on Io and Europa continuously repave their surfaces.
Callisto's surface is much older, likely because the moon itself is older than Io or Europa.
The moon is farther out in its orbit than the others, which explains why it gets struck more often.
questions.why: More craters means an older surface. All three moons are the same age, but volcanism on Io and ice activity on Europa keep erasing craters, while geologically dead Callisto keeps every one.

questions.q: Suppose you discover chasms on a rocky exoplanet that stretch for hundreds of kilometers. The planet has no substantial atmosphere but is twice as massive as Earth. Which is a reasonable hypothesis for the origin of the chasms?
options: They are a result of impacts to the surface from asteroids coming in at a glancing blow.
They are a result of erosion, as these planetary conditions permit a water cycle.
They are a result of volcanism, as lava flows can carve deep channels in softer rock.
They are a result of tectonic activity, as internal heat is likely high enough for large-scale surface disruption.
They are a result of atmospheric processes such as storms that can crack the landscape.
questions.why: A planet twice Earth's mass keeps plenty of internal heat, so tectonic stretching and cracking of its crust is likely. With no atmosphere there is no water cycle or storms, so erosion and weather are ruled out.

questions.q: On what kind of world would we expect to see evidence of erosion?
options: On a large planet far enough from its host star to freeze water, with a high rotation rate (short day) and lots of atmosphere.
On a small planet close enough to its host star to vaporize water, with a slow rotation rate (long day) and little atmosphere.
On a large planet at a suitable distance from its host star to allow multiple phases of water to coexist, with a high rotation rate (short day) and lots of atmosphere.
On a small planet far enough from its host star to freeze water, with a high rotation rate (short day) and little atmosphere.
On a large planet at a suitable distance from its host star to allow multiple phases of water to coexist, with a slow rotation rate (long day) and lots of atmosphere.
questions.why: Erosion needs weather: a thick atmosphere (large size helps hold one), water that can rain, flow and freeze, and fast rotation, which drives strong winds and storms.

questions.q: Which of the following is by itself NOT evidence for plate tectonics on Earth?
options: Seismic data shows that most strong earthquakes happen along long fault lines that connect together, dividing Earth's surface.
Some continental boundaries, and especially their continental shelves, fit together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle.
Numerous mountains and active volcanoes are found across the Earth's surface.
Similar rocks and fossils are found in different continents.
Satellites detect incremental movement of different large landmasses.
questions.why: Mountains and volcanoes alone do not prove moving plates: Mars and Venus have them without plate tectonics. Linked earthquake belts, fitting coastlines, matching fossils and measured drift all point to plates.

questions.q: Mid-ocean ridges are places where
options: hot mantle material rises upward and spreads sideways, pushing the plates apart.
one plate sinks beneath another, returning older crust to the mantle.
plates slip sideways relative to one another.
hot mantle material rises upward, creating volcanic islands.
plates push together, creating ocean mountain chains.
questions.why: At mid-ocean ridges hot mantle rock wells up and spreads outward, making new sea floor and pushing plates apart. Sinking beneath is subduction; sideways slipping is a transform fault; rising plumes making islands are hot spots.
